steps.title: The two forms
steps.html:
Both forms connect the past to now. The difference is what you are pointing at.

The present perfect simple (have/has + past participle) points at a result. It answers how many?, how much?, what has changed? The activity is over, or the number is final: I’ve written three letters this week.

The present perfect continuous (have/has been + -ing) points at the activity and the period it has filled. It answers how long?, what have you been doing? It often implies the activity is unfinished, or that its traces are still visible: I’ve been writing letters all morning.

Compare: She’s read your letter (she knows what it says) and She’s been reading your letter (she may still be halfway through it).

steps.title: Four rules to hold on to
steps.html:
• State verbs stay simple. be, know, own, believe, mean, understand, belong — I’ve known her for ages, never I’ve been knowing.
  • With live, work, study, teach plus for or since, the two forms mean much the same: She’s worked / She’s been working here since 2019.
  • for + a length of time; since + a starting point. for twenty years, since 2009.
  • A finished time expression kills both forms. I wrote to her yesterday, not I’ve written to her yesterday.

steps.title: Text A · What the numbers actually say
steps.html:
Written for this course. Figures from Ofcom, Post Monitoring Report (UK postal regulator).

For most of the last two decades, the story of the letter has been a story of subtraction. Ofcom, the body that regulates post in the United Kingdom, has been counting addressed letters since before the smartphone was ordinary: in 2011 the system carried around 14.3 billion of them, and the figure has since fallen to roughly 6.6 billion. Nothing dramatic has caused this. No government has banned the postage stamp. Volumes have simply been sliding, year after year, at close to nine per cent, and every attempt to reverse the trend has failed.

The obvious explanation is that we have stopped writing, and the obvious explanation is wrong. Thanks to digital media, most of us produce more words before lunch than our great-grandparents wrote in a month. What has changed is not the writing but the surface it lands on. A message arrives — instant, weightless, free — and is read and deleted inside a minute. An email sits in an inbox until somebody clears it. Nothing has waited in an in tray for a fortnight since about 2003.

The postal systems themselves have been adjusting to the arithmetic rather than fighting it. Denmark has given up its guarantee of nationwide letter delivery altogether. In 2025 the British regulator allowed second-class letters to be delivered on alternating weekdays rather than six days a week, because a network built for fourteen billion items cannot be paid for by six. None of these decisions has been popular, and none of them has been reversed. The letter is not being killed off by anyone. It is being quietly priced out of the ordinary week.

steps.title: Text B · The half of a life that used to be written down
steps.html:
Written for this course.

Historians have been pointing at the consequence for some time. Almost everything we know about ordinary life two centuries ago, we know from correspondence — from letters that nobody at the time thought were important, kept in boxes by people who were not thinking about history at all. For four hundred years that evidence has been quietly accumulating. It has now stopped. A biographer working in 2150 will have millions of public posts to read and almost no private ones, because the confidential half of a life has moved onto servers that are designed to forget.

There is a second loss, and it is harder to measure. A handwritten page carries information that no screen reproduces. You can see where the writer has crossed out a word and chosen a better one, where the handwriting has speeded up towards the end of a difficult sentence, where the pen has pressed too hard. Punctuation does a little of that work in a typed message, and an emoticon does a little more, but neither shows you a person changing their mind in front of you.

None of this has gone unnoticed. Sales of stationery have been climbing in several markets for years, and the shops report that the buyers are not nostalgic pensioners but customers under thirty — people who have never queued for a postage stamp in their lives. Letters have been reappearing wherever slowness is an advantage rather than a fault: in hospitals, in prisons, between grandparents and grandchildren. None of it has rescued the post, and it was never going to. But something has changed all the same. “I’ve been meaning to drop you a line for ages” was once an apology. It has quietly turned into a promise.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
I have been writing to the same person for twenty-six years, and for most of that time I have not thought about it at all.

It started with a school exchange in 1999. We wrote on paper because there was nothing else: a letter every few weeks, a postage stamp I had to ask my mother for, my terrible handwriting, whole lines crossed out where I had changed my mind halfway through a sentence. I still have every one of hers in a box. I have never once opened it.

Since about 2008 we have been messaging instead, and the exchange has become both constant and weightless. We speak far more often than we ever wrote, and I could not tell you a single thing we have said this year. Everything is instant; nothing is kept. I have been meaning to write to her properly for ages.

I know exactly what has changed. The correspondence has not stopped. It has simply stopped leaving a trace.
